power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We argued initially that decisions made in the process of test development would have accounted for the multitude of structures of masculinity within different measures (see Table 1). Accordingly, we suspected the emergence of bloated specifics, that is, pseudo-facets of masculinity that occurred due to the over-representation of particular item contents (Cattell & Tsujioka, 1964). We expected this structural heterogeneity to account for, at best, modest intercorrelations among composite scores of masculinity measures. Contrary to this notion, composites of masculinity measures elicited very high intercorrelations and a high agreement between the correlation profiles with external variables (see Table 2), suggesting that the overall scores actually tap into the same construct. At first glance, however, the host of correlation differences with external constructs stands out. That said, closer inspection reveals that many correlation difference tests were significant even in the case of comparatively small numerical differences. This can be explained by high intercorrelations between the compared scores and the relatively large sample size, both of which mostly exceeded our assumptions for the a priori power analysis: More specifically, over-sampling (ntarget = 1,020; nempirical = 1,077) and slightly stronger than expected intercorrelations among masculinity measures occurred (rtarget = .70; rempirical, median = .76). Both aspects increased the statistical power to detect differences we deemed negligible (Δr ≤ .10; cf. Gignac & Szodorai, 2016). For instance, the composite scores of the Male Role Norms Inventory and the Conformity to Masculinity Norms Inventory were correlated with the compassion facet of agreeableness at rs = -.43 and -.35, respectively, and this difference was significant at p < .001 because the two masculinity measures were correlated at r = .69.

On the one hand, our hypotheses H1 to H10 require bivariate correlation analyses. On the other hand, our intended tests of jingle and jangle fallacies rested on comparisons of the correlation profiles of masculinity measures, openness, right-wing authoritarianism, and social dominance orientation, utilizing tests of correlation differences for dependent correlations (Steiger, 1980). A Monte Carlo simulation (k = 5,000) carried out with the R package diffcor (version 0.8.4; Blötner, 2024) revealed a required minimum sample size of 1,020 participants to detect a correlation difference as large as |r| ≥ .10 (which corresponds to a small effect), given a target power of 1-β = .80, one-sided testing, a Type I level α = .001, and an intercorrelation between the compared scores as large as r = .70. We chose the mentioned Type I error level to account for multiple testing and the related issues of αaccumulation. The assumed intercorrelation between the compared scores reflects the average correlation between two measures of classical masculinity as detected by Sanders et al. (2024). The aforementioned sample size also warrants a statistical power of 1-β = .80 to detect an interaction effect (as proposed in H12) as small as f² = .022, given α = .001.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps > .001", Text = "As can be seen, in most cases, masculinity measures did not elicit substantial percentages of incremental validity beyond each other when it comes to accounting for variance of the external criteria, most ps > .001."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "ps > .001", Sentence = "As can be seen, in most cases, masculinity measures did not elicit substantial percentages of incremental validity beyond each other when it comes to accounting for variance of the external criteria, most ps > .001."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: A plethora of adaptive features concomitant with the endorsement of such norms has been identified, such as career advances, striving for success, and reproductive success, but also maladaptive features such as poorer mental health, higher engagement in risky health behaviors, lower propensity to seek psychological help, and a higher tendency to resort to violence (e.g., Di Bianca & Mahalik, 2022; Horton et al., 2026; Levant et al., 1992 Levant et al., , 2020;; Mahalik et al., 2003; Thompson et al., 1992; Walker et al., 2000).

text.text: Although all empirical studies and theoretical frameworks employ the same umbrella term, they differ regarding the scope of features of masculinity.

Such conceptual heterogeneity suggests the existence of a jingle fallacy (cf. Thorndike, 1904); that is, the erroneous assumption that the same construct is measured across different frameworks because all apply the label masculinity.

text.text: That is, "meeting societal expectations for what constitutes masculinity in one's public or private life" (p. 3).
The endorsement of masculinity as per these conceptualizations goes along with specific affects, behaviors, and cognitions (see Thompson et al., 1992).

text.text: The conceptualizations differ, however, with respect to the motivational underpinnings concomitant with the endorsement of masculinity norms.

That is, Levant et al. (1992) underscored other-ascribed masculinities (i.e., what men should do according to societal standards), whereas Mahalik et al. (2003) referred to self-ascribed masculinities (i.e., the degree to which an individual conforms to these standards; Wong & Wang, 2022).

This research evaluated whether masculinity research is affected by a jingle fallacy.
Furthermore, we evaluated whether the masculinity construct is indeed a unique construct or whether its contents are already covered by broader already existing constructs.

Cases in which the same construct is propagated with different names ("Old wine in new bottles") are commonly referred to as a jangle fallacy, that is, the erroneous assumption that two measures or constructs would differ because they bear different names (Kelley, 1927).

text.text: If the masculinity construct turns out to be redundant with closely related yet broader constructs, further research on the masculinity construct would no longer be justified as it would reflect a waste of resources for parallel strands of research (Flake & Fried, 2020).

text.text: From a methodological stance, disparate conceptualizations (or factor structures) may-at least in part-be explained through the use of pre-structured item sets that were subsequently subjected to exploratory factor analyses.

In this regard, inspections of the item pools suggest the emergence of bloated specifics therein, that is, spurious factors occurring in exploratory factor analyses because specific contents are relatively over- 1 We would like to thank an anonymous reviewer for this illustration of conceptual differences.

Therefore, latent factors can emerge because of the similarity of the items rather than conceptual coherence (Cattell & Tsujioka, 1964).

text.text: Our inspections revealed that many measures of the endorsement of masculinity norms repeat essentially the same content multiple times, which favors the extraction of pseudo-factors.

For instance, the Heterosexual self-presentation subscale from the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory (Mahalik et al., 2003) entails the items "It would be awful if people thought I was gay", "I would be furious if someone thought I was gay", and "I would get angry if people thought I was gay", all of which are essentially redundant.

text.text: Similarly, the Toxic Masculinity Scale (Sanders et al., 2024) includes the items "If I cry, I am weak", "Crying means I am weak", and "Expressing sadness publicly makes me weak" that constitute emotional restriction.

text.text: That said, it is trivial that the factor emerging from a set of items is determined by the breadth of the item contents subjected to analysis, with a broader set likely constituting a higher number of latent factors.

Moreover, if researchers subject to analysis a pre-structured set of items that they deem representative of a target construct, the subjective considerations that guided the development of items will inevitably favor specific factor solutions.

In other realms of psychological assessment, however, test construction endeavors usually rest on a more explicit theoretical foundation than is the case in masculinity research in which the target concept is defined by itself (e.g., conformity to masculinity as meeting social standards associated with masculinity [Mahalik et al., 2003]) and where no clear framing exists about which aspects do or do not reflect features of masculinity.

text.text: This conceptual uncertainty has implications for construct validity.

That said, hardly comparable conceptualizations, only moderate correlations among operationalizations, and ambiguous relations with pertinent criteria lend initial support to the existence of a jingle fallacy (Lawson & Robins, 2021).

text.text: In the remainder of this manuscript, we refer to harmful and toxic masculinity constructs collectively as problematic masculinities.
Their respective authors purported to pinpoint the harmful effects of the concepts that-in their views-have not yet been sufficiently acknowledged by classical masculinity concepts.

At first glance, however, the definitions of harmful masculinity as "detrimental beliefs that perpetuate rigid, hetero-normative, violent, and controlling norms about what a 'real man' is" (Hill et al., 2020, p. 2) and of toxic masculinity as "the overemphasis and indulgence in societal-based masculine traits to an extent that is harmful to oneself and/or others" (Sanders et al., 2024, p. 3) add little beyond the definition of classical masculinities because all agree in terms of prescriptive and proscriptive social pressure imposed on men to behave in a certain way.

text.text: Thus, the question arises whether broader, more general constructs readily cover the endorsement of masculinity norms.

More specifically, we argue that the endorsement of masculinity norms must be distinct from the lower pole of openness to experience (hereafter openness) as per the Big Five model, as well as from right-wing authoritarianism and a social dominance orientation.

Akin to both classical and problematic conceptions of masculinity, low openness and right-wing authoritarianism include adherence to conventional mindsets (Beierlein et al., 2015; Costa & McCrae, 1992).

text.text: This focus on hierarchies is reflected in measures of masculinity as well, such as in the power over women subscale of the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory (Mahalik et al., 2003) and the negativity toward sexual minorities subscale of the Male Role Norms Inventory (Levant et al., 2007).

text.text: Low openness, social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism tap adherence to conventional rules and endorsement of intergroup inequality rather broadly.

The endorsement of masculinity norms is comparatively narrower and focuses on conventions that regard men's behavior, women's roles, disdain for homosexuality, and the enforcement of heteronormativity.
That is, the conventional rules and endorsed group inequalities regard very specific social groups.

Accordingly, it stands to reason that the endorsement of masculinity norms can be subsumed under at least one of the three aforementioned personality features, such that the endorsement of masculinity norms reflects a more specific version of low openness, a social dominance orientation, or right-wing authoritarianism. text.text: Many previous studies that claimed to have identified or refuted assumed jingle or jangle fallacies rested on bivariate correlations between operationalizations of the constructs under scrutiny.

However, this approach confers only little information because the magnitude of a single bivariate correlation coefficient depends on a host of features, such as sufficient variance of the involved test scores and the degree to which the scores are affected by a measurement error.
As a reaction, semi-standardized guidelines have been proposed for detailed statistical evaluations of jingle and jangle fallacies (Blötner, 2025; Lawson & Robins, 2021).

text.text: These guidelines rest on comparisons of the nomological networks of two or more competing test scores (e.g., for classical and problematic masculinities).
If the test scores in fact tap the same underlying construct, their nomological networks should be highly similar.
To this end, a reasonable set of external constructs must be identified that is suitable to either separate or unite the concepts under scrutiny.
A jingle fallacy among classical masculinity conceptualizations would be indicated if operationalizations thereof exhibited-by and large-different strengths of associations with external constructs.

A jangle fallacy, in turn, would be indicated if classical and problematic masculinities, for instance, elicited-by and large-similar relations with external constructs (Blötner, 2025; Lawson & Robins, 2021).

In the following, we justify the selection of external constructs with which we construct the nomological networks of masculinity measures and derive the accompanying hypotheses.
Therein, we address both construct validity and criterion validity.
Of note, each of the following hypotheses is tested for each measure for the endorsement of masculinity norms.

In the formulation of the hypotheses, we assumed that the same patterns held for rightwing authoritarianism and a social dominance orientation, given that we tested whether these two constructs essentially include the endorsement of masculinity norms.
For openness, we proposed the opposite pattern of associations, given that we tested whether low openness includes the endorsement of masculinity norms.

We did not formulate correlation difference hypotheses, as recommended by the framework by Blötner (2025), because in many cases, we had no reason to assume that two particular masculinity scores, for instance, would be differently correlated with a given construct.

text.text: At first glance, one might expect that men strongly endorsing masculinity norms are equipped with better mental health.
Consistent evidence exists, however, according to which individuals scoring high in masculinity report poorer rather than better mental well-being.
This pattern is usually interpreted along the line of denial of psychological health issues and the ostensible ideal of a "real men" displaying toughness.
In line with these findings, we hypothesized that scores of masculinity measures would be positively related to perceived stress (H1) and mental health issues (H2).
Moreover, masculinity concepts emphasize that "a real man" would resort to violence if it serves his goals (e.g., Di Bianca & Mahalik, 2022; Harrington et al., 2021; Horton et al., 2026).

text.text: To this end, we administered an imaginary and adapted version of the dictator game.

In the standard form of the dictator game, one participant (the dictator) receives an endowment and unilaterally decides how much to keep and how much to give to a passive recipient, who has no power to refuse the allocation.

text.text: We constructed broad nomological networks by assessing a host of external criteria.

Then, we tested the similarities between the correlation patterns of masculinity measure, openness, right-wing authoritarianism, and a social dominance orientation both at the local and at the global level.

At the local level of analysis, we tested whether the total scores of masculinity measures, openness, right-wing authoritarianism, and a social dominance orientation were differently correlated with any external construct (e.g., a need for power), considering the correlation between the compared measures of the compared constructs.
At the global level of evaluation, we quantified the overall similarities among the correlation profiles, spanned by all validation criteria, with a single index.
Therein, we pursued the fundamental logic of nomological networks: If two scores yield similar associations with other measures, the two scores likely measure essentially the same construct.

Thus, a jingle fallacy among classical masculinity measures could be ruled out if the corresponding measures exhibit a small number of meaningful correlation differences with external measures, along with high overall agreements between the observed correlation profiles.

Applied to comparisons between (a) classical and problematic masculinity measures, (b) between classical masculinity measures on the one hand and either openness, or social dominance orientation, or right-wing authoritarianism, or (c) between problematic masculinity measures on the one hand and either openness, or social dominance orientation, or right-wing authoritarianism, in turn, negligible correlation differences and high agreements among the correlation profiles would indicate a respective jangle fallacy (Blötner, 2025).

text.text: Thus, examinations at the level of subscales do not sufficiently exploit the rich information of the total scores.

Moreover, structural differences and commonalities between conceptualizations of masculinity that account for disparate subscale structures would also be reflected in the comparisons of the nomological networks of the overall scores.

Comparisons at the level of the subscales of, for example, the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory and the Male Role Norms Inventory are not eligible due to unique, albeit to some extent overlapping, subscale structures.

This problem concerning internal structures is further exacerbated when comparing seemingly more distal conceptualizations, such as the multidimensional Male Role Norms Inventory and the unidimensional Man Box Scale.
To assess the degree to which these configurations converge in the sense of jingle or jangle fallacies, we deem evaluations at the level of the total scores mandatory.

We asked the participants to imagine being allocated a sum of 100€ (approx. $100), which they have to share with another person who cannot intervene.
The participants decided on their own how much money they would share, while there would only be one trial and no opportunity for renegotiation.
Therein, the gender of the fictitious recipient was manipulated randomly such that the pseudo-receiver was either presented as another man, as a woman, or as a nonbinary person.
From the final sample, 348, 349, and 380 participants played the dictator game with a fictitious nonbinary person, with a fictitious man, and with a fictitious woman, respectively.

We recorded the sum offered to the virtual respondent as an index of prosociality toward members of different gender groups, with a proposal of 0€ meaning that players would keep the whole sum for themselves (i.e., maximal egotism) and a proposal of 100€ meaning that players would give the whole sum to the receiver (i.e., maximal altruism).
Offers could be made in steps of 1€.

text.text: Lawson and Robins' (2021) guidelines for the evaluation of assumed jingle and jangle fallacies propose the evaluation of the uniqueness versus redundancy of two constructs (in our case, traditional and problematic masculinities) by comparing one-factor and two-factor solutions in a confirmatory factor analysis.
We added this procedure as a non-preregistered analysis to further obtain evidence for or against our claim of the existence of jingle and jangle fallacies in masculinity research.

We used the R package lavaan (version 0.6-21; Rosseel, 2012) to investigate whether a one-factor solution (indicating a jangle fallacy) or a two-factor solution (with distinct but correlated traditional and problematic masculinity factors) would fit better to our data.

text.text: We did so by specifying two forms of models, namely item-level and parcel-level models, each of which was furthermore tested with hierarchical and non-hierarchical structuring: In the item-level, non-hierarchical variant, we assigned all items directly to the overarching factors (i.e., broad masculinity in the single-factor model; classical and problematic masculinity in the two-factor model).

In the item-level hierarchical variants of the single-and two-factor models, we considered the multidimensional structures of all measures by assigning items to their corresponding subscales (as proposed by the original authors), subscales to their corresponding measures, and measures either to (a) an overall factor or (b) to classical or problematic masculinity factors.

In the corresponding parcel-level variants, we specified subscale-wise parcels for each measure and assigned these parcels either to scale-level high-order factors (i.e., hierarchical) or directly to broad factors.
We compared fit indices between the corresponding variants and evaluated the latent correlations in the two-factor models.

text.text: To improve conceptual clarity in masculinity research, this research set out to examine jingle and jangle issues in the research area of the endorsement of masculinity norms.

First, heterogeneous conceptualizations of the endorsement of masculinity implied that existing measures for this phenomenon tapped into disparate constructs (Smiler, 2004; Thompson & Bennett, 2015; Thompson et al., 1992; see also Table 1).

text.text: Third, regardless of the label used, empirical endeavors to justify the uniqueness of the masculinity construct in light of the existence of established yet conceptually broader constructs such as openness, social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism were quite simplistic and rested on exaggeratedly strict tenets.

In addition, we sought to add to our argument by running non-preregistered tests of mutual incremental validity, which further informed our analyses of jingle and jangle fallacies.

Most cases in which at least moderate levels of mutual incremental validity occurred regarded characteristics with high centrality for the understanding of the effects of the endorsement of masculinity, such as traditional views on society (reflected through right-wing authoritarianism), a social dominance orientation, a need for power, mental health, and proactive aggression (Di Bianca & Mahalik, 2022; Mahalik et al., 2003).

text.text: Altogether, strong intercorrelations, numerous negligible correlation differences with external constructs, the extremely high similarity between the total correlation profiles, and mostly negligible levels of mutual incremental validity in predictions of external variables render our initial suspicion about a jingle fallacy for overall scores of classical masculinity measures untenable.

Instead, the composite scores of two tested measures for the assessment of the endorsement of masculinity norms mostly tap the same underlying phenomena, regardless of the underlying structure, because virtually the same conclusions concerning our hypotheses held for the overall scores of the Male Role Norms Inventory and the Conformity to Masculinity Norms Inventory.

More specifically, and consistent with the notion of a tough self-display and the denial of negative sensations (Addis & Mahalik, 2003; Mahalik et al., 2007; Parent et al., 2011), the overall scores of the endorsement of masculinity norms as per the aforementioned measures went along with higher stress experience and poorer mental health.

For instance, although the Male Role Norms Inventory includes item content aimed at low display of emotionality (facet entitled restrictive emotionality; see Table 1), endorsement of masculinity norms as per the composite of the Male Role Norms Inventory was less strongly correlated than other masculinity measures with scores of neuroticism and stress symptoms.

In this regard, it must be noted that the aforementioned measures differ with respect to the assumed origins of the perceived pressure to comply with masculinity norms.

More specifically, the items from the Male Role Norms Inventory emphasize perceived external drivers (i.e., other-ascribed masculinity), whereas the items of the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory pinpoint an individual's own desire to adhere to masculine standards (Levant et al., 1992; Mahalik et al., 2003).

text.text: Considering the wordings from the two measures of problematic masculinity, it stands to reason that the corresponding "standards" also reflect fundamental beliefs of an individual rather than norms that were predominantly imposed on this individual.

Differences in the suggested extrinsic (versus intrinsic) origins of the norms or standards captured in the measures likely accounted for the smaller effect sizes observed for the Male Role Norms Inventory.

At the same time, our analyses suggest that the two measures purported to measure what we refer to as problematic masculinity (Toxic Masculinity Scale and Man Box Scale) add little beyond classical masculinity: Beyond the uncertainties related to the conceptual novelty derived from the underlying definitions (see above), their composite scores exhibited extremely strong correlations with the composite scores of classical masculinity measures, elicited predominantly negligible correlation differences vis-à-vis external constructs, their overall correlation profiles virtually mirrored those of classical masculinity measures, and they yielded substantial incremental validity only in a few cases (see Tables 2 and 3).

text.text: Such conceptual and psychometric redundancy fragments the literature and stalls meaningful theoretical progress.

Addressing this jangle fallacy is therefore essential to equip researchers and practitioners with the precise tools needed to further our understanding of modern masculinities and the societal as well as mental health implications concomitant with the endorsement of strict masculinity norms (e.g., Haslop et al., 2024; Love et al., 2025).

text.text: Last, our findings did not suggest that overall scores of any conceptualization of masculinity were reducible to low openness to experience, a social dominance orientation, or right-wing authoritarianism.

Despite certain conceptual overlaps, the endorsement of masculinity norms reflects domain-specific prescriptive norms about motives, goals, and behaviors allegedly deemed prototypically male (e.g., status, power, heteronormativity).

text.text: Of note, our hypotheses that build on offers made in the dictator game could not be supported.
That is, neither was any masculinity measure significantly correlated with overall offers made, nor was this relation moderated by the gender of the recipient.

We argue in this regard that the imaginary setting of the dictator game did not afford the desired demand characteristics an incentivized dictator game would have engendered, limiting ecological validity.
Given the absence of advantages related to egotism, most participants did not make unfair offers (see the distribution of offers in our Open Science Framework supplement).

This pattern is consistent with the study by Zhao et al. (2017) in which participants kept more money to themselves if they played for real money rather than being asked to only imagine the redistribution scenario.

text.text: Thus, incentivization may have altered the patterns of offers made.

Interestingly, in this regard, offers made to an imaginary female interaction partner were significantly higher than offers made to imaginary male (d = 0.34, 95% CI [0.23, 0.44]) or nonbinary interaction partners, d = 0.31, 95% CI [0.20, 0.42] (see our supplement).
We suspect that the manipulation of recipients' gender reflected a demand characteristic towards gentlemanly behavior.

More specifically, participants may have perceived social role expectations that request men to showcase benevolence towards women (Gough & Novikova, 2020), and thus, social desirability may have been at play (Komlenac et al., 2023).

text.text: Alternatively, participants could have resorted to benevolent sexism.
These considerations are highly speculative, however, given the low overall variance in observed offers in our dictator game.

Furthermore, no single item in our item pool could be used as a proxy for the endorsement of "gentleman norms" or benevolent sexism, which could have served as a moderator in the relationship between the endorsement of masculinity norms at large and offers made to recipients with different genders.
Future research might, therefore, test whether such tendencies moderate the relationship between the endorsement of masculinity norms and prosociality towards women.
Note that in the aforementioned sections, we highlighted that all conclusions drawn from our data refer to overall or composite scores of the endorsement of any masculinity concept.
We applied our analyses to overall scores to ensure that the corresponding contents assigned to the same broad umbrella term-masculinity-are comparable across conceptualizations.

This being said, the respective facets proposed in the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory and the Male Role Norms Inventory usually do not constitute comprehensive overall masculinity factors as many facets frequently yield only small or even negative correlations among each other (Levant et al., 1992; Mahalik et al., 2003; Wong & Wang, 2022).

text.text: Bifactor analyses of the Conformity to Masculine Norms Inventory and the Toxic Masculinity Scale indicated that no comprehensive general factors-besides the corresponding specific factors-can be assumed for these measures.

In contrast, the Male Role Norms Inventory and the Man Box Scale constitute meaningful overall factors, as suggested through good model fit for single-or bifactor models along with high loadings onto the corresponding general factors (see our Open Science Framework supplement).
As such, the emergence of a general factor reflecting the endorsement of masculinity norms depends on the utilized measure.

This notion opposes previous claims according to which it would be misleading to compute overall scores of masculinity measures because they would not constitute such general factors (Wong & Wang, 2022).

text.text: Another caveat regards convergence issues in the preregistered analyses of the common factor structure of classical and problematic masculinities.

By means of common confirmatory factor analyses, we sought to establish whether classical and problematic masculinities are better understood as two (at best moderately) correlated factors or as one comprehensive factor.

Our non-preregistered standalone confirmatory factor analyses of each measure were already confronted with specific challenges, such as failure to establish general factors for some of the masculinity measures.
These issues related to each measure per se further exacerbate the emergence of comprehensive problematic versus classical masculinity factors or even a comprehensive general masculinity factor.

We would like to note, however, that (a) the manifest overall test scores of the masculinity measures exhibited very high correlations among each other (rs ≈ .70 and above), (b) virtually identical nomological networks occurred for the overall scores of the four measures, and (c) the overall scores of the measures yielded only limited mutual incremental validity beyond each other.
Notably, the inability to successfully estimate the proposed latent structure does not invalidate the remaining analyses.

Therefore, we argue that claims about the same construct being measured by the overall scores of the four masculinity measures can also be made without confirmatory factor analyses emphasizing the superiority of a single-factor model or findings of two extremely highly correlated latent factors (cf. Blötner, 2025; Lawson & Robins, 2021).

Last, our study purposefully addressed the redundancy of the administered masculinity measures at the composite score level to capture the entirety of masculinity standards of each conceptualization.

Using even larger and more diverse samples, future work would arguably benefit from employing latent variable approaches that more directly evaluate the extent to which all available measures reflect common versus unique variance (e.g., bifactor or related structural models).

Such approaches may provide a more direct test of whether these instruments primarily reflect a common masculinity factor or whether meaningful specific dimensions remain after accounting for shared variance.

Our findings provide clear evidence that overall scores of toxic and harmful masculinity do not constitute constructs that can be distinguished from overall scores computed for classical masculinities.

Instead, composites of toxic and harmful masculinity concepts align almost perfectly with composites of classical masculinity measures, indicating a jangle fallacy at least at the level of the global measures.
In contrast, suspected jingle issues among composites of classical masculinity measures were not supported.
Despite structural differences, total scores of classical measures exhibited very high intercorrelations and nearly identical patterns of associations with external constructs.
These results indicate that global scores of classical masculinity tap the same underlying construct.
Simultaneously, they offer theoretical value beyond broader traits such as openness, social dominance orientation, and right-wing authoritarianism, from which they were clearly distinguishable.

The non-incentivized and imaginary nature of the applied variant of the dictator game likely limited behavioral differentiations, suggesting that future work should incorporate incentivized or other ecologically valid behavioral measures.
What has not yet been evaluated in detail regards the existence of redundancies versus distinctions at the level of the facets of classical, harmful, and toxic masculinities.
The search for a comprehensive structure from all available contents was beyond the scope of this research, but it remains a promising outlook for future studies.
In this regard, we encourage consolidation rather than further expansion of masculinity constructs, alongside future work that incorporates behavioral indicators.
Likewise, cultural and measurement-invariance issues should be addressed to strengthen construct validity in masculinity research.
